questions.q: What is wrong with this log line?
questions.hint: Can a machine pull the order number out of this sentence? And whose data is going into the log?

options.text: The message differs every time, so the event is hard to group or count
options.why: With variables inside the message, every line is a different message to a machine. A fixed message (order.paid) would be countable.

options.text: The order ID isn't in its own field, so filtering needs regex
options.why: The fact is baked into the sentence. With order_id in the context you could filter on it directly.

options.text: The customer's email (personal data) goes into the log
options.why: A user_id is enough to identify someone. An email in a log is visible to many people and stored for a long time.

options.text: The info level is wrong: every payment log should be at error level
options.why: A successful payment is normal, so info is right. Use error only when something broke and someone needs to look.

questions.q: Sarah's API logs all carry a correlation ID, but the email worker's logs don't, so she can't find out why an email never went out. What is the right fix?
questions.hint: The worker is a separate process. How would it learn the number held in the request's memory?

options.text: Generate a new ID in the worker for each message
options.why: A new ID separates the worker's logs, but it never links them to the API's logs. The story stays broken.

options.text: Attach the ID to the message as a stamp when dispatching, and read it back in the worker
options.why: The number crosses the queue with the message. One Messenger middleware handles both directions.

options.text: Match the API's and worker's lines by timestamp
options.why: Hundreds of messages run in the same second, and a worker may act long afterwards. Time can't match them reliably.

options.text: Set the worker's log level to debug
options.why: You get more lines, but still no way to tell which line belongs to which request.

questions.q: Eric's team passes correlation_id by hand in every logger call, and sometimes forgets. What is the best fix?
questions.hint: What runs by itself just before every log record is written?

options.text: Prepend the ID to the message as a string
options.why: Then the message is no longer fixed and the ID isn't in its own field, so both filtering and grouping get harder.

options.text: Write a Monolog processor that adds the number to every record
options.why: Written once, it applies to every line in every channel. Nobody has to remember anything.

options.text: Add the ID only to error logs
options.why: The story before an error is in the info lines. Without the number on them you can't piece it together.

options.text: Make it a strict code-review rule that nobody may forget
options.why: People will forget. Anything a machine can guarantee shouldn't depend on human memory.

questions.q: A request coming through the API gateway already has an X-Correlation-Id header. What should your service do?
questions.hint: When a package moves from one hub to another, does it get a new tracking number?

options.text: Validate the value's format, then use it
options.why: With one number, the gateway's and your service's logs line up. Validation keeps junk out of your logs.

options.text: Always create a new ID, so your service owns its own
options.why: That breaks the chain: the gateway's logs and yours can no longer be found under one number.

options.text: Put whatever arrived into the log as it is, without validating
options.why: Users can send headers too. Without validation, huge or forged text ends up in your logs (log injection).

questions.q: Sarah wraps her HTTP client so the correlation header is added in one place. Which call will still go out without it?
questions.hint: What exactly did she decorate?

options.text: A call made through a separate scoped client that was not decorated
options.why: A decorator on http_client covers only that service. Each scoped client is its own service and needs the same wrapping.

options.text: A call made through the default client in a controller
options.why: The default client is exactly what the decorator replaces, so these calls get the header.

options.text: A call made through the default client inside a worker
options.why: Same service, same decorator. The worker has already made the stamp's number current.

questions.q: Checkout sometimes takes 4 seconds. The path includes the API, a database, a payment service and a queue, and nothing shows an error. What shows most directly where the time goes?
questions.hint: What measures the duration of each step separately?

options.text: The error log
options.why: Slow is not an error. Nothing broke, so the error log has nothing.

options.text: The server's CPU graph
options.why: Waiting on an outside service uses no CPU. The graph stays calm while the request is slow.

options.text: The trace of the slow request, with the time of each span
options.why: With every span's duration side by side, the longest step jumps out immediately.

options.text: Add more debug logs everywhere and deploy again
options.why: You might find it eventually, but slowly and by guesswork. A trace gives you this measurement ready-made.

questions.q: Which of these are safe to put in a log context?
questions.hint: Which ones, if leaked, would let someone steal money or take over an account?

options.text: order_id and user_id
options.why: These are internal identifiers. You can't search without them, and nobody outside can do anything with them.

options.text: The payment gateway's name and the error code
options.why: This is what you need to understand the problem, and there is nothing secret in it.

options.text: The token from the Authorization header
options.why: Anyone holding the token can call the API as that user. Then everyone who can read logs has that power.

options.text: The full card number
options.why: Keeping card data in logs is a direct PCI DSS violation, and a leak means financial loss.

options.text: The password the user entered
options.why: A password should never sit in plain text anywhere, not even in the database, let alone in a log.

questions.q: The system gets 2,000 requests per second. What is the problem with storing every request's full trace, and what is the usual remedy?
questions.hint: Do you really need every trace to find the slow requests?

options.text: No problem, keeping all traces is the rule
options.why: Sending and storing every span of every request means huge data volumes, cost and extra load on the app.

options.text: It costs a lot and adds load, so you sample and keep only a share of traces
options.why: Keeping 10% of 2,000 requests a second is still 200 traces a second, plenty to spot slow and broken requests, at a tenth of the cost. The price: a particular request may not have been kept.

options.text: Drop traces and keep only logs
options.why: Logs say what happened but not how long each step took. The two do different jobs.

questions.q: Matt's dashboard shows a green 100ms average latency, yet some customers say checkout "hangs". Which measure should he look at first?
questions.hint: Which measure catches the few slowest customers?

options.text: p99 latency of the checkout route
options.why: It shows the experience of the slowest 1% of customers, which drowns in the average.

options.text: The server's average CPU
options.why: The CPU can be low while requests are slow because they wait on an outside API or a lock.

options.text: The total request count
options.why: A count tells you about traffic, not slowness.

options.text: The average again, over a longer period
options.why: However long the period, an average keeps hiding the few slow customers.

questions.q: Which of these pairs a measure with the right metric type?
questions.hint: Which one only goes up, and which one moves up and down?

options.text: orders_placed_total: counter
options.why: Total orders only go up; rate() gives you the rate.

options.text: queue_depth: gauge
options.why: The number of messages waiting right now rises and falls.

options.text: request_duration_seconds: histogram
options.why: Durations are counted into buckets so you can get percentiles.

options.text: active_connections: counter
options.why: Connections open and close, so the value goes down too. That is a gauge.

questions.q: What is the problem with this metric code?
questions.hint: How many different values could these labels take?

options.text: The full path and userId as labels: countless time series, cardinality will explode
options.why: Label bounded values like the route name (order_show) and status; never IDs.

options.text: inc() should be incBy()
options.why: inc and incBy are both fine. The problem is the label values.

options.text: There should be no method label
options.why: method is bounded (GET, POST...), so it is safe as a label.

questions.q: The RED dashboard is all green, yet emails aren't arriving because a worker is stuck. Which metric would have caught it first?
questions.hint: The API is answering, but where is the work piling up?

options.text: Queue depth (saturation) and the age of the oldest message
options.why: Piled-up work is the direct sign of something stuck.

options.text: The API's p50 latency
options.why: The API answers fast because it just drops the job on the queue. The problem is behind it.

options.text: The total request count
options.why: That shows traffic, not stuck work.

options.text: Total disk space
options.why: Space isn't the problem here; the worker process is.

questions.q: The team sets checkout's SLO at 99.9% (30 days). This month 40 minutes of failure have already happened. What should they do?
questions.hint: How big is the budget, and how much has been spent?

options.text: The budget is about 43 minutes and nearly all is gone. Pause risky features and focus on stability
options.why: By the rule agreed in advance, when the budget runs out you reduce risk.

options.text: Nothing; 40 minutes is less than an hour
options.why: The limit is 43 minutes, so only 3 minutes remain.

options.text: Change the SLO to 99% so there is budget again
options.why: Lowering the target after missing it hides the real problem. A target comes from what customers need.

options.text: Shut the whole service down until the month ends
options.why: Shutting down causes even more failure. The goal is to reduce risk, not to stop the service.

questions.q: Rachel's metrics code works on her laptop, but in production under PHP-FPM every scrape shows tiny, resetting counts. What is the likely cause?
questions.hint: How long does one PHP-FPM request live?

options.text: The registry uses in-memory storage, which dies with each request
options.why: Each request is a fresh process, so its counters start from zero. Redis or APCu storage keeps them between requests.

options.text: Prometheus scrapes too often
options.why: The scrape interval changes how fresh the graph is, not whether the values survive between requests.

options.text: Counters should have been gauges
options.why: The type is not the problem. A gauge in memory would be lost the same way.

questions.q: The 99.9% checkout SLO is burning at 14.4 times the allowed rate. If nothing changes, roughly how long until the 30-day budget is gone?
questions.hint: Divide the window by the burn rate.

options.text: About 2 days
options.why: 30 days / 14.4 is about 2 days (50 hours). That is why this burn rate pages someone.

options.text: About 30 days
options.why: 30 days is how long it would last at exactly the allowed rate (1x).

options.text: About 14 hours
options.why: It mixes up the burn rate with hours. The window divided by the rate gives about 50 hours.

questions.q: Which of these make good SLIs?
questions.hint: Does this number capture the customer's experience?

options.text: Checkout requests answered within 500ms without a 5xx / all checkout requests
options.why: It directly captures the success and speed the customer sees, as one ratio.

options.text: The share of time the server's CPU stays under 80%
options.why: CPU is a machine measure; customers can fail even while the CPU is low.

options.text: Successful logins / all valid login attempts
options.why: It counts valid attempts only, leaving out wrong passwords and bots, so the ratio is honest.

questions.q: The endpoint below is used as a liveness probe. What is wrong?
questions.hint: What will this probe do when the database goes down?

options.text: When the database goes down, liveness fails and every server restarts, yet a restart doesn't fix the database
options.why: Liveness must not include dependencies. Checking the DB is the readiness endpoint's job.

options.text: It should use Response instead of JsonResponse
options.why: The response type isn't a problem.

options.text: "SELECT 1" is slow, so a more complex query is needed
options.why: The issue isn't the type of query but the purpose of the probe.

options.text: Nothing wrong: with no database, there is no point in the app staying alive
options.why: The app is alive and will work again when the database returns. A restart only loses in-flight work and warm caches.

questions.q: Which dependencies belong in readiness?
questions.hint: What can the app not handle a single request without?

options.text: The main database
options.why: Almost no request succeeds without it, so traffic is better off going to another server.

options.text: A third-party email service
options.why: Email can wait in a queue and be sent later. Taking every server out because of its outage is overkill.

options.text: Session or cache (Redis), if the app depends on it
options.why: In an app that relies on login, nothing works without Redis, so this is an essential dependency too.

options.text: An advertising or analytics service
options.why: An optional service. The customer's work goes on without it.

questions.q: What should happen when a readiness probe fails?
questions.hint: Will the process die?

options.text: The load balancer stops sending traffic to that server, and sends it again once it recovers
options.why: The server isn't shut down; it just rests for a while.

options.text: The server restarts immediately
options.why: That is liveness's job. Readiness only controls traffic.

options.text: The new deploy is canceled
options.why: It can hold up a deploy's rollout, but it doesn't cancel it.

questions.q: Which of these alerts deserve a page?
questions.hint: Is customer harm happening right now?

options.text: Checkout errors above 5% for 5 minutes in a row
options.why: A symptom, urgent, and there is something to do (roll back or investigate).

options.text: Payment success rate suddenly drops from 99% to 80%
options.why: The money path is broken. Customers are directly harmed, so page.

options.text: Disk usage passed 60%
options.why: It grows slowly and isn't urgent. A ticket or a predictive alert fits.

options.text: One worker restarted
options.why: It heals itself and no human has anything to do.

questions.q: Brian's team gets 300 alerts a month and nobody reads them anymore. What should they do first?
questions.hint: On which alerts did anyone actually do something?

options.text: Count how often each alert led to action, and delete or demote to tickets the ones nobody acted on
options.why: Cutting the useless alerts gives the rest their weight back.

options.text: Make every alert ring louder on the phone
options.why: The problem isn't volume but quantity and relevance.

options.text: Add more alerts, so nothing is missed
options.why: More alerts means more noise, and the real ones get buried further.

options.text: Tell on-call to switch their phone off at night
options.why: Then nobody wakes up for a real fire either.

questions.q: Which part of this alert rule is directly tied to the runbook?
questions.code:
- alert: CheckoutErrorsHigh
  expr: error_ratio > 0.05
  for: 5m
  labels: {severity: page, team: payments}
  annotations:
    runbook_url: 'https://wiki.shop.example/runbooks/checkout-errors'
questions.hint: Where does the on-call person go after being woken up?

options.text: annotations.runbook_url
options.why: It puts the link to the instructions one click from the alert.

options.text: for: 5m
options.why: That is a waiting time, not instructions.

options.text: labels.severity
options.why: That is the level of urgency; it doesn't say what to do.

questions.q: At 3 a.m. checkout gets 4 requests in 5 minutes and 1 fails. The rule "error ratio above 5% for 5 minutes" pages. What is the best fix?
questions.hint: One failure out of four is 25%. What is missing from the rule?

options.text: Add a minimum-traffic condition, such as more than 12 requests a minute
options.why: With almost no traffic a single error looks huge. The floor skips these moments and still pages when real traffic fails.

options.text: Raise the threshold to 50%
options.why: A real outage at 30% errors in the busy hour would then go unnoticed.

options.text: Remove `for: 5m` so it reacts faster
options.why: That makes it noisier, not quieter.

options.text: Turn the alert off at night
options.why: Customers also buy at night, and then a real failure would wake nobody.

questions.q: Sarah's app was deployed at 14:00, and from 14:10 30% of payments fail. What is the best first step?
questions.hint: Stop the harm first, find the cause later.

options.text: Roll back that deploy, then look for the cause
options.why: A recent change is the likeliest cause, and a rollback is fast and safe.

options.text: Log into the live server, dig through the suspect code and fix it directly
options.why: The harm continues, and a direct change brings new, untracked risk.

options.text: Tell the customers and wait
options.why: Telling them is needed, but alongside stopping the harm, not instead of it.

options.text: Turn on more logging and watch
options.why: Investigation comes later. When you know about a recent change, stop the harm first.

questions.q: Which incident should be treated as SEV1?
questions.hint: Is there direct harm to money or data?

options.text: Checkout is down for all customers
options.why: Revenue stops directly: the highest urgency.

options.text: Users' personal data may have leaked
options.why: Data is at risk and there is legal liability too (for example 72 hours under GDPR). SEV1.

options.text: The admin report page is a little slow
options.why: An inconvenience to the internal team, no customer harm. SEV3.

options.text: A small typo on the website
options.why: At the very bottom of the priorities; a ticket.

questions.q: Nicole's deploy renamed customer.phone to mobile in one migration and checkout failed. She rolled the code back and it still fails. Why?
questions.hint: What did the rollback not touch?

options.text: The old code asks for phone, but the database already renamed it
options.why: Rollback swaps the code only; the schema stays as the migration left it.

options.text: The rollback did not restore any code
options.why: It did restore the old code. That is exactly why it now asks for a column that is gone.

options.text: The cache must be cleared before a rollback works
options.why: A stale cache is a different problem; the error here is a missing column.

options.text: She should have waited longer for the rollback to finish
options.why: Waiting changes nothing; the code and the schema disagree.

questions.q: An incident is under way. Two developers are changing prod at the same time and neither knows what the other is doing. What is the best fix?
questions.hint: Who is coordinating?

options.text: Appoint an Incident Commander; every change goes through them and is written in one channel
options.why: The changes stop canceling each other and everyone knows what is going on.

options.text: Let whoever started first carry on and have the other stop, without telling them why
options.why: Without knowing who is doing what, this fails too; you need a coordinator.

options.text: Let both carry on; one of them will fix it
options.why: This way the changes keep undoing each other.

options.text: Call everyone in and add more people
options.why: More people means more chaos, if there is no coordinator.

questions.q: Ethan's status update says: "Some issues, looking into it." Why is that weak?
questions.hint: What did the manager learn from reading it?

options.text: The impact isn't in numbers, it doesn't say what is being done, and there is no next-update time
options.why: A good update has the impact, what we know, what we're doing, what we don't know and the next time.

options.text: It shouldn't have been written in that language
options.why: Language isn't the problem; the content is vague.

options.text: There should be no update at all; fix the problem first
options.why: Without updates everyone phones the developer. Giving updates is the Comms lead's job.

questions.q: Which of these postmortem lines is in the blameless spirit?
questions.hint: Which one gives you something to fix?

options.text: "Ryan deleted production with the wrong command."
options.why: The blame lands on one person. There is nothing to fix, and the next person could make the same mistake.

options.text: "Production and staging commands look the same and there was no confirmation step, so the mistake was easy to make."
options.why: It names a weakness in the system, and fixes follow from it (a different color, confirmation, permissions).

options.text: "We need to be more careful."
options.why: A wish, not an action. With no owner or date, nothing will change.
